entries.title: The Composer
entries.summary: In the Review’s October 22 issue, Matthew Aucoin surveys Philip Glass’s six-decade musical career, occasioned by the premiere of his new symphony, Lincoln, at Tanglewood this past summer. “Any artist who invents a distinctive, instantly recognizable mood is sure to leave a mark on the history of their art form,” Aucoin writes. “And Glass did […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

In the Review’s October 22 issue, Matthew Aucoin surveys Philip Glass’s six-decade musical career, occasioned by the premiere of his new symphony, Lincoln, at Tanglewood this past summer. “Any artist who invents a distinctive, instantly recognizable mood is sure to leave a mark on the history of their art form,” Aucoin writes. “And Glass did invent a mood, one that feels inseparable from American urban life in the late twentieth century.”

For twenty-first century American life, the classical music world may look to Aucoin, who, when he is not writing about Thomas Adès, Pierre Boulez, and the state of music criticism for the Review, is primarily a composer and conductor. His operas, including Eurydice and Crossing, have been performed everywhere from New York’s Metropolitan Opera to the Los Angeles Opera, and the Metropolitan’s Eurydice was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Opera Recording in 2023. Aucoin was also the recipient of a 2018 MacArthur Fellowship. A studio recording of his operatic work Music for New Bodies will be released later this month.

This week I emailed Aucoin to ask him about the rigors of performing Philip Glass’s concatenating arpeggios and the pleasures of putting poetry to music.

Daniel Drake: I have an indelible memory of seeing the Philip Glass Ensemble at the Ravinia Music Festival outside Chicago about twenty years ago, and there was a woman sitting in a chair on stage doing nothing for the first thirty minutes of the performance, until finally she sang one long, high note a few times, and then, in my memory at least, returned to silence. Anyway, as you note in your essay, performing Glass’s music can be a particular kind of challenge. Have you ever performed or played one of his compositions? What was the experience like?

Matthew Aucoin: I’ve performed a reasonable amount of Glass’s music over the years, as a conductor and as a pianist. I’ve played some of his piano études; I conducted his opera Akhnaten in Los Angeles, with my friend Anthony Roth Costanzo, the countertenor, in the title role; and I’ve conducted some of his vocal chamber music, also with Costanzo.

You have to adjust your inner clock, your inner sense of time, when you perform Glass. Or at least I do: I find myself generally more at home performing music that has a playful, quicksilver sensibility, music that’s full of surprises and that can turn on a dime from one mood to another, whether it’s Mozart or Thomas Adès or whoever. With Glass, you have to train yourself to feel larger units of time: a phrase might repeat sixteen or thirty-two times, and you have to feel that whole span of time as a single gesture, not a million swirling notes.

It makes all the difference in the world whether the people performing the music love and believe in it. Costanzo, for instance, has become one of the world’s great Glass performers; you feel, when you perform with him, that he’s slowed down his metabolism to match that of the music. He’s undergone some kind of quasi-monastic training. I have a suspicion that when he sings Akhnaten he subsists entirely on sunlight; the guy may have mastered photosynthesis.

And I’ve performed Glass’s études alongside pianists, like Timo Andres, who inhabit the music so deeply that they’ve found ways to be creative with it, to stretch its phrasing from within, the way you would with late Brahms. But if you perform Glass’s music with an orchestra that has no experience with it or sympathy for it, sometimes the main thing on the string players’ mind is the risk of tendonitis.

Where and how did you first encounter Glass’s music, that you remember?

I have no idea. By now his music is everywhere, it’s in the American ether. I probably encountered some Glass knockoff (hard plastic?) in a movie soundtrack or TV commercial before I heard the real thing.

In Geoffrey O’Brien’s 2022 review of your Eurydice, he notes your “insistently vigorous score full of quick changes and fleeting stylistic intrusions of everything from Philip Glass to tango music,” and on listening to it this week, I seemed to pick up on snatches of minor-key arpeggios and the kind of percussion one sometimes encounters in a Glass work. Did you consciously incorporate any of his style into your opera, or—and forgive my ignorant ear—are there explicit references to his Orphée? Or do you think it’s just a matter of composing After Philip, as it were? 

Another eminent composer once wrote to me saying, in effect, “don’t worry if people compare something of yours to Philip Glass, that happens to everyone and it means nothing.” I touched on this in my essay: if you make use of the humble and ancient arpeggio, which surely belongs to us all, people will instantly think of Glass.

Advertisement

There’s texture, and then there’s process. It’s easy to recognize likenesses of texture between different composers. But what matters more is the musical process, how musical material (harmony, timbre, etc.) evolves in time. And when it comes to process, my music has nothing to do with Glass’s. I would make a terrible minimalist! For better or worse, in my music, one idea tends to follow another pretty swiftly, and I have my hands full trying to weave them into something coherent. At his best, Glass is patient—a quality I admire.

What music are you working on now? Are there any subjects or ideas you’re working through?

A project that’s especially close to my heart, and that’s consumed my energy for the past few years, is about to be released: the recording of my piece Music for New Bodies, which is a vocal symphony or nonnarrative opera based on recent poems by Jorie Graham. That album will come out through DACAMERA Editions on October 30.

Graham’s poetry—as readers of The New York Review will know—somehow manages to reckon with the whole spectrum of human existence in the 2020s. And maybe not only human existence: some poems seem to be spoken by nonhuman presences. One features the oracular voice of the bottom of the ocean, who has frightening things to say to our species; and in several poems, there’s an unsettling collective voice, like a swarm of bots. (The word “bot” suddenly looks antiquated, doesn’t it? Even they have been replaced, by “agents.”)

Anyway, it changed my life, to immerse myself in this polyvocal poetry and find a way to set it to music. The director Peter Sellars, who staged the piece’s first production last year, also worked with me on assembling the libretto, and Peter is a force of liberation.

There’s a mysterious liminal zone of musical works that are neither concert pieces nor operas. They’re music-theater works, but they resist the conventions of the theater. Glass’s Einstein on the Beach lives in this zone. And I found that it activated something new in my music, to write a music-theater piece that wasn’t a tidy narrative, where you’re not constantly thinking about plot, but where the music could be the guiding force.

What music are you listening to right now?

Can I admit something embarrassing? I don’t listen to that much music at home. I compose music all day, and then usually the last thing I need is to hear more notes. Often I just want the pablum of a good podcast. However, one new album that I’ve found totally mind-expanding—inventive and virtuosic and without any precedent that I know of—is my friend Keir GoGwilt’s Zarabanda Variations, which takes the music of colonial New Spain (present-day Mexico) as a jumping-off point for a musical voyage that’s dazzling and dislocating and fabulously weird.

entries.title: Edwin Frank on Love and Death in the American Novel
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In this episode of Private Life, Edwin Frank joins Jarrett Earnest to discuss Leslie A. Fiedler’s Love and Death in the American Novel (1960), which was reissued by NYRB Classics in April. They discuss the preoccupations of Fiedler’s literary criticism, the process of putting together a collection of criticism, and Frank’s book Stranger than Fiction: Lives of the Twentieth Century Novel (2024).

Edwin Frank is the editor of New York Review Books as well as the founder and editorial director of the NYRB Classics series. In addition to Stranger than Fiction, he has also released a collection of poems, Snake Train (2015).

Leslie A. Fiedler (1917–2003) was a literary critic and novelist. He published two novels and three short story collections, as well as dozens of volumes of criticism, including The Stranger in Shakespeare (1972), Freaks: Myths and Images of the Secret Self (1978), and Fiedler on the Roof: Essays on Literature and Jewish Identity (1991).

Next week’s episode will be a selection from Love and Death in the American Novel, read by the writer Rachel Kushner. You can find Love and Death in the American Novel at nyrb.com or at your favorite bookseller.

entries.title: Ming Smith’s Ming Smiths
entries.summary: Perhaps the most obvious thing in our surroundings which is an occasion for “unselfing” … is what is popularly called beauty. … I am looking out of my window in an anxious and resentful state of mind, oblivious of my surroundings, brooding perhaps on some damage done to my prestige. Then suddenly I observe a […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Perhaps the most obvious thing in our surroundings which is an occasion for “unselfing” … is what is popularly called beauty. … I am looking out of my window in an anxious and resentful state of mind, oblivious of my surroundings, brooding perhaps on some damage done to my prestige. Then suddenly I observe a hovering kestrel. In a moment everything is altered. The brooding self with its hurt vanity has disappeared. There is nothing now but kestrel.

—Iris Murdoch, The Sovereignty of Good (1970)

Ming Smith’s self-portraits are not of the self as it is usually understood: one’s own person, separate and apart. The difficulty lies in the term self-portrait. Each word on its own suggests singularity and enclosure. The self, contained. The portrait, framed. The compound feels even more tight and fixed and flat, as if the hyphen between the two words were a connector piece between blocks or a tiny arrow tracing the absorption of a living being into a static thing: self → portrait.

But, put simply, there are often other people in Smith’s works of that name: Self-portrait with Harlem Boys Choir (1980s); Self-Portrait, Sophisticated Ladies, Phyllis Hyman and Judith Jamison (1980s); Self-Portrait, Just Above Midtown, In the Presence of Lynda Goode Bryant (1980s). In the eerie Gemini Self Portrait (Hart Leroy Bibbs) (1980s), is Smith with her twin? In all of these so-called self-portraits, the artist is in the presence of others; she acknowledges this in her titles; she naturalizes it with her lovely clothing, which always suits the social occasion. These are her people; she is with; she is among. In ubuntu philosophy, “I am because we are”—or as a Harlem sister might put it, “I am because we be.”

In Smith’s black-and-white 1986 Self-Portrait (Total), her son breastfeeds on her lap while she holds the camera over his hidden head, her geometric shirt pulled down, her arms a cubistic frame, her hair a soft nest around this hasty Madonna and Child. In Self-Portrait, Ming and Mingus (1992), he’s still on her lap but he has grown and his gaze at us is slant. The title now announces the self twice (thrice via the Ming in Mingus), but in a way that dissolves the self rather than emphasizes it. Smith’s camerawork says: I am only because of and through others.

Even in the more exactly self-portraits of Smith alone, there is a quality of displacement, a jarring loose of the self, a slippage between the photographer and the photographed. Other self-portraitists use tricks, tripods, timers to conceal the apparatus and the artifice. Smith tends to hold the camera in her hands, in front of her face or body. Every time we see a camera in a photograph, we deduce a mirror, which must have stood where we now stand—except that Smith is never quite looking at us. The eye becomes a lens. The window to the soul, a hall of mirrors. The mirror-stage, a dramatic one.

Roland Barthes notes that this multiplicity underlies every photographic portrait, which is “a closed field of forces [that] intersect here, oppose and distort each other. In front of the lens, I am at the same time: the one I think I am, the one I want others to think I am, the one the photographer thinks I am, and the one he makes use of to exhibit his art.” A photographic self-portrait adds another I to this array: the one the photographer herself thinks she is. Imagine. In front of the lens, all those selves, at the same time. Ming Smith’s selves-portraits, then.

Or maybe, given how these selves intersect, oppose, and distort one another in the force field, Ming Smith’s un-self-portraits. I take the idea from Iris Murdoch, who draws our attention to how the experience of beauty, a quality that art and nature share, can occasion an “unselfing,” a change of consciousness. Smith’s self-portraits thrum with beauty. They belong to art and nature alike. They unself us the way the glimpse of a hovering bird through a window can, in Murdoch’s words, “clear our minds of selfish care.”

Smith’s Hidden Self-Portrait and Green (1980s) enmeshes subject, window, and nature in Murdoch’s scene of seeing, layering them in a way that draws the eye out of the self and into the murky world. We make out a silhouette in glass, elbow up and active; she stands before or behind a black thicket, a greenish glow aching from below. There are echoes here of Smith’s “Memphis in Morningside” series—women in nature’s tangled shadows—but also of her “Hidden Swan” series and of Woman and Red Curtain (1980s): smooth figures curving out of darkness, catching the blue light of gloam or dawn, annihilating all that’s made till every thought becomes a shade.

Advertisement

Ming Smith’s unselfing-portraits, then. But that is still wrong—portraits etymologically por-tray, draw forth, pull out, disclose. Smith’s photographs don’t participate in this logic of capture and revelation, of closing and opening a box. We find instead a sense of being flung into life, what philosophers have called the thrownness, errantry, or fugitivity of existence.

In her gorgeous sidelong black-and-white Self-Portrait (ca. 1988), Smith tilts back and seems to have just swung the camera up, precarious in her hands. In Self-Portrait with Olympus (1990s), the camera is suspended mid-whim—eyes dim, hair in a towel, breast bare but for the glint of a thin, gold chain. The self is a passing thought after the shower. Each of these images is less a composed portrait than a motion among motions.

The characteristic trails and smudges of light that tremble over Smith’s work always lend it this thrilling vibrancy. In Self-portrait in Blur (1980s), from the “Yemayá” series, the orisha’s sacral energies are converted into wild and radiant lines: kinetic coronas, solar flares. Ming Smith’s unselfing-sketches, then? No, sketch is too bare a word. Especially for these photographs, where that vibrational vitality takes on the vibrancy of color—color at the speed of light, that is, always searing and smearing, flashing and receding.

We again see the difference color makes in Smith’s extraordinary series of self-portraits as Josephine Baker. A black-and-white version from 1986 camouflages Smith into Baker’s Jazz Age folies with surreal collaged animals and faded newspaperly grittiness. In the color trials, we see Smith herself in her professional capacity as a model, posing like a cross between a hieroglyphic queen and a “material girl” of the 1980s, bedecked in jewel tones and a spiraled wire bustier, and, in one shot, in Baker’s iconic, ironic banana skirt—but with real fruit.

Smith in her vocation as an artist is all over these images, too, especially the test-shots, which carry traces of her labor: the selection and design and forging of the costumes; the mounting of the stage and the backdrop to scatter the iridescence of the plastic we wrap bouquets in; the setting up of the lights and the camera, outside the frame this time. As Josephine, she seems directly to channel rather than perform Baker’s self-glamourizing, her auto-ornamentation, even her satirical nudity.

In the most naked of these shots, Smith Betty-Boops at us, feet bare, gold skin peeking from behind and between the gaudier gold of her jewelry and drapery. A long loop of pearls wraps around her wrist and hand, then dribbles between her breasts into the shiny folds below. Another loop swoops from the crook of her other elbow and is caught mid-swing, pearls dotting and grooving the air. The effect is a quivering stillness, a spectacular intimacy.

The paradox of Smith’s glamour—she is both the artist and the work of art, both subject and object—is on full display in this series. The word glamour comes from a word that originally meant enchantment, a slippage from the word grammar, which in its medieval sense could apply to scholarship or occult learning. There’s voodoo in glamour: the one who possesses it, who is glamorous, partakes in knowledge and conjuring power.

What is the grammar of glamour? I put a spell on you, because you’re mine. Does the incantation of glamour transform me? Bewitch you? Or enthrall us? In Smith’s self-portraits as Josephine, is she the enchanter, the enchanted, or the spell itself? How many selves?

Smith seems to solve rather than succumb to Barthes’s paradox of the photographic portrait:

What I want, in short, is that my (mobile) image, buffeted among a thousand shifting photographs, altering with situation and age, should always coincide with my (profound) “self ”; but it is the contrary that must be said: “myself ” never coincides with my image; for it is the image which is heavy, motionless, stubborn… and “myself ” which is light, divided, dispersed; like a bottle-imp, “myself ” doesn’t hold still, giggling in my jar: if only Photography could give me a neutral, anatomic body, a body which signifies nothing!

Instead of a thousand shifting photographs, photographs of a thousand shifts. Instead of the self caught inside the portrait, the two in a staggered dance. (I think of Shadow Self (Imprint).) Instead of a heavy and stubborn image at odds with a light and divided self, a sensuous negotiation between them. Stillness itself, but dispersed and imp-like, giggling out of the bottle of the self, ajar. A furious spirit, beside herself, whirling into an incandescent nothing. An I split into the many-eyed gaze of the we.

entries.title: The Wexford Touch
entries.summary: Among all the music and opera festivals of Europe, Salzburg might be the grandest, or it certainly thinks it is; the Schwarzenberg Schubertiade is the prettiest, with Schubert played and sung amid the lovely hills of the Bregenzerwald overlooking the upper Rhine; and Bayreuth is without doubt the most grueling. Richard Wagner characteristically decreed that […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Among all the music and opera festivals of Europe, Salzburg might be the grandest, or it certainly thinks it is; the Schwarzenberg Schubertiade is the prettiest, with Schubert played and sung amid the lovely hills of the Bregenzerwald overlooking the upper Rhine; and Bayreuth is without doubt the most grueling. Richard Wagner characteristically decreed that the audience must suffer for his art, and spend sixteen hours listening to the Ring while seated on acutely uncomfortable wooden benches.

But the Wexford Festival Opera, which marks its seventy-fifth anniversary later this month, is surely the unlikeliest: an annual gathering founded by local enthusiasts in a small town in the southeast corner of an Ireland that was then far from prosperous. Since my first visit in 1969 I’ve become very fond not only of the festival but of the place. Wexford has around 20,000 inhabitants, a handsome front on the estuary of the River Slaney, two huge Victorian Catholic churches and a modest Georgian protestant church, and a fascinating history, much of it somber.

The Romans never conquered Gaelic Ireland, but it was the Vikings who founded Wexford as well as Waterford, Limerick, and Dublin in the ninth and tenth centuries. In 1169 Anglo-Norman knights led by “Strongbow”—Richard de Clare, Earl of Pembroke—landed in Wexford at the invitation of Dermot MacMurragh, the deposed king of Leinster. (Strongbow’s subsequent marriage to MacMurragh’s daughter Aoife is gloriously depicted in Daniel Maclise’s 1854 painting in the National Gallery in Dublin.) Later centuries saw terrible events. Oliver Cromwell’s army massacred the townspeople of Wexford during his near-genocidal campaign in Ireland in 1649; the rebellion of 1798 was savagely repressed, ending with the last stand of the Wexford rebels on “Vinegar Hill, the fatal conclave,” as Seamus Heaney wrote in his poem “Requiem for the Croppies.”

Despite the oddity that the first performance of Handel’s Messiah was in Dublin in 1742, Ireland has a sparse history of classical music and opera, at least when compared with many other European countries, or for that matter with Ireland’s extraordinary literary tradition, up to this day. Wexford is the birthplace of the novelist John Banville and the playwright Billy Roche, author of a trilogy set in his hometown; Colm Tóibín, born in Enniscorthy fifteen miles up the Slaney, went to school there and now writes opera librettos of his own, including for one of this year’s Wexford premieres, Alberto Caruso’s The First Festival, commissioned to mark the institution’s anniversary. But Wexford was the last place anyone would have expected to hear opera.

Nor would they have but for one man. Tom Walsh was an anaesthetist at the local hospital, a man of great charm and a zealous opera-lover. Operaphiliacs tend toward the obsessive and esoteric, and the two-volume history of The Monte Carlo Opera by Dr. Tom, as we all knew him, is about as esoteric a subject as could be. But then perhaps only an eccentric and a dreamer could have achieved what he did.

When he dreamed of staging opera in Wexford he can’t possibly have imagined the success and international réclame it would one day enjoy. By happy chance there was a long-forgotten Theatre Royal, a Georgian building on the High Street—the misleading name of a street of row houses which isn’t wide enough for two cars to pass—which had long been disused, or rather used as a storehouse. Under Dr. Tom’s guidance it was cleared out and restored and fitted with 550 seats, in time for the first festival to open on October 21, 1951.

For its first night Wexford gave a patriotic choice, The Rose of Castille by Michael William Balfe, a Dubliner who is not much now remembered. By contrast the next year’s opera was one we all know and love, L’Elisir d’amore, followed by Don Pasquale the year after that. These began a Wexford tradition of performing Donizetti, twenty of whose operas have by now been given, to the delight of those of us who can’t get enough of him. Not only was Dr. Tom the begetter of the festival, he remained artistic director for fifteen years, and after that still the genius loci, who used to give us sherry on Sunday mornings.

In the early days of the festival Ireland seemed a long way from Europe and Wexford a remote destination, and not only geographically. Under the very long dominance of Éamon de Valera Ireland languished economically and culturally, with a powerful Roman Catholic church and a strict censorship of books and movies, if not of operas. Soon, however, Wexford was able to lure English and continental artists. In 1958 Anna Bolena, Donizetti’s opera about Henry VIII’s unfortunate wife, was conducted by Charles Mackerras, then in his early thirties and on his way to becoming one of the great conductors of his time. He wasn’t then commanding the fees he would later expect, and since Wexford couldn’t possibly compete financially with the larger opera houses—Royal Opera, Scala, or Met—it developed considerable skill in finding artists early in their career. In that Anna Bolena the critic of the London Times picked out Fiorenza Cossotto as “a mezzo-soprano at the beginning of a great career,” words which could have been used a year later when Rossini’s La Gazza Ladra was given at Wexford with a small part taken by the mezzo Janet Baker, then only twenty-six but later to become a very great artist, and very much loved.

Advertisement

In 1969 I was working not very fruitfully in my first job, in what would be a brief and inglorious career in publishing. I was already absorbed by opera, and after I heard about the forthcoming Wexford festival I made my first journey, five hours by train to the southwest extremity of Wales and then three hours in the ferry to Rosslare. I didn’t foresee that Wexford would become part of my life, but I’ve returned every year since, apart from the lockdown year of 2020, when the festival was held virtually.

Among the pieces I heard that first year was Haydn’s L’infedeltà delusa. Haydn put his genius into his string quartets and his talent into his operas, largely written to entertain Prince Esterhazy’s court, and this was a pleasing piece of fluff. But it was enlivened by two wonderful singers, the soprano Jill Gomez, who died recently, and Ugo Benelli, a true tenore di grazia in the tradition of Tito Schipa, and a Wexford favorite.

One of the pleasures of Wexford has been watching careers unfold. The celebrated opera director David Pountney’s first professional production—of Janáček’s Katya Kabanova—was in Wexford in 1972. Three years later it was at Wexford that Jane Glover—later to become, among other things, the third woman to conduct at the Met—conducted for Cavalli’s Eritrea in her first professional performance. The enchanting soprano Christiane Eda-Pierre, from Martinique, delighted Wexford with her shimmering voice and idiomatic French style in Delibes’s Lakmé and Bizet’s Pêcheurs de perles, some years before she was singing Gilda at the Met with Pavarotti. The festival’s tradition of finding them young continued into the next century: in 2017 Luigi Cherubini’s Medea was given in an unsatisfactory production (to put it politely) by Fiona Shaw, but with the title part sung by Lise Davidsen, who demonstrated the thrilling top of her voice. Within a few years she would be the most sought-after dramatic soprano of the age, from London to New York, where she is presently exciting audiences in the Met’s production of Verdi’s Macbeth.

And Wexford also proved to be a nursery of intendants. Brian Dickie was artistic director when I arrived, and in the fullness of time he ran the Chicago Opera Theater, while Elaine Padmore was a successful artistic director at Wexford in the 1980s before she went on to Copenhagen and then the Royal Opera in London. None was more remarkable than David Agler, an American-turned-Canadian (before that became more fashionable!) conductor as well as administrator, who conducted four operas at Wexford while also running the show. Seeing Si j’étais roi by Adolphe Adam in 2000 under his baton is a particularly happy memory. So was hearing Ferdinand Hérold’s opéra comique Le Pré aux clercs in 2015. Hérold’s work was not only charming in itself, but Agler had put on something you will almost never hear today in any country, including France, which is to say an opera in French sung by an entirely native Francophone cast, idiomatically conducted by Jean-Luc Tingaud.

No festive atmosphere could disguise the fact that some Wexford evenings have been better than others. Wexford hasn’t escaped the curse of Directors’ Opera, where the director treats the work as something to play with or deconstruct, however little the result has to do with what the composer and librettist intended. Indeed at one point there seemed a convention that one out of the three Wexford performances would be all right, one would be pretty awful, and one would be terrific. The quality of the operas themselves has been similarly uneven. Even a really good performance in 2016—including a spellbinding Rosalind Plowright as the Old Baroness— could not persuade me that Samuel Barber’s Vanessa was ever destined for immortality. But then again in 2013 we had a real discovery, Jacopo Foroni’s 1849 Cristina, regina di Svezia (which would come in handy if, during a high-grade operatic quiz evening, the question asked for the names of operas about the queens of France, of Sweden and, two of them, about Elizabeth the First of England), admirably conducted by Andrew Greenwood and with a gripping performance by Helena Dix in the title part.

Advertisement

With Wexford’s growing success the audience began to change. Memory plays tricks, but I recall in the 1970s a mixture of Anglo-Irish (“the Descendancy,” the decayed but civilized survivors of the old Protestant ascendancy), cultivated Monsignori, and cosmopolitan aesthetes. In the decades that followed Ireland saw burgeoning prosperity, though also notable economic inequality, and the audience increasingly came from the newly well-to-do of Dublin. By the new century Wexford had outgrown the original theater and it was decided to build a new one, although ingeniously concealed behind the same modest facade. When the new house opened in 2008, after a season held in a large tent in the grounds of a nearby castle, it became one of the best theaters of the age in Europe, comparable with the splendid new opera house at Glyndebourne. By a lamentable misfortune the opening coincided with the financial crash, which hit Ireland particularly hard. Mercifully the festival, like the country itself, survived the bleak years that followed and prospered again.

So far I haven’t conveyed what gives Wexford its special quality as a place to visit yearly. Beyond the good craic—as the Irish say—there has always been a particular sense of a gathering of friends, where singers mingle with visitors. In 1971 Il re pastore, Mozart’s frivolous piece of juvenilia, was performed with such excellent singers as Anne Pashley and Norma Burrowes. With not much time before the first night the set still wasn’t quite finished, and the designer Elisabeth Dalton enlisted her friend Rodney Milnes—opera critic of the Spectator for years and then the Times, and my companion on countless nights at the opera for more than forty years—to help paint the scenery, along with myself. This remains my only practical contribution to the Wexford Festival Opera.

And still it’s quite true what they say: Wexford is fun—and that is not a word that has ever been used by those trudging up the Grüner Hügel at Bayreuth towards Wagner’s temple to his art and himself. Years ago now one critic wrote that Wexford was what Salzburg must have been like in the 1920s. That was when creators worked together for the joy of it and the audience was made up of enthusiasts, rather than an array of the international rich. You could say that about Wexford to this day.

entries.title: A Delicate Repair
entries.summary: The late Nigerian sculptor Erhabor Emokpae is perhaps best known for his bronze replica of the sixteenth-century ivory mask of Queen Idia, the kingdom of Benin’s premier iyoba, or queen mother. The year was 1977. Nigeria had attained political independence from Britain less than two decades earlier and been through a bitter civil war in […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
The late Nigerian sculptor Erhabor Emokpae is perhaps best known for his bronze replica of the sixteenth-century ivory mask of Queen Idia, the kingdom of Benin’s premier iyoba, or queen mother. The year was 1977. Nigeria had attained political independence from Britain less than two decades earlier and been through a bitter civil war in the late 1960s. Seeking to prove its stability and assert its influence on the continent, the young country hosted the Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture (FESTAC)—at the time the largest gathering of artists from Africa and its diaspora ever convened. Emokpae’s mask, cast from a carving by the lesser-known artist Pa Joseph Alufa Obgayabona, served as the emblem of the event.

The festival’s national committee chose Queen Idia as a powerful precolonial symbol of resilience: believed by some to be the force behind the throne during her son Ésigie’s reign, she led armies to defend Benin’s sovereignty. After her death, Ésigie commissioned masks to memorialize her by Benin’s bronze and ivory casting guilds. But the selection was also a response to the British Museum’s effective denial of Nigeria’s request to borrow the original mask a year earlier. The piece had come into the museum’s custody as a spoil of war; for its return on loan, the museum asked Nigeria to pay 2 million naira ($3 million) plus insurance, the equivalent of more than $16 million today. The young country refused. Emokpae’s replica—forged to replace the stolen original—symbolized Nigeria’s defiance of their former colonizers’ demands.

Emokpae was born in Benin City, once the heartland of Benin’s empire—which at its sixteenth-century peak stretched as far east as the Niger River and almost as far west as present-day Accra in Ghana, an area roughly one fifth the size of modern Nigeria. He made the mask particularly for the people of his home region, for whom the theft of the original was part of a larger story about the colonial looting of what are known as the Benin Bronzes, a collection of several thousand masks, sculptures, and other carvings made between the thirteen and nineteenth centuries, primarily of brass but also of ivory, coral, and other materials. Britain pillaged these items from Benin’s royal palace in 1897, taking them to defray the cost of what is still remembered in the region as a humiliating massacre. The Benin monarchy has been appealing to the British government to return the artifacts since at least the 1930s, emphasizing that they are not merely treasure but expressions of a people’s history.

If the desire to reclaim the bronzes has long united many Nigerians, the effort to do so has also been a reminder of Benin’s uneasy place in the federal republic. While colonialism disrupted most regional social and political structures in West Africa, Benin’s monarchy persevered; a single family line has held onto the crown for over eight centuries and today maintains ceremonial importance and political influence, despite lacking a formal function in governance. When Nigeria gained independence in 1960, Benin retained a distinct identity.* Many of the local Bini people understood themselves to be newly subject to the Nigerian state much as they had previously been ruled by the British crown. After the British Museum refused to loan out the Queen Idia mask, Akenzua II, the oba, or king, is said to have told Nigerian government officials that “Benin’s forefathers made the first bronzes, and they’d do it again.” The comment expressed pride in his ancestors’ aptitude—but it also seemed to emphasize his kingdom’s claim to the artifact over that of the postcolonial state’s.

Nearly half a century later, these tensions have come to a head with the return of many of the bronzes. Though the British Museum has continued to deny Nigeria’s requests, other museums in the UK, US, and Europe, along with private donors, have collectively agreed to send back over a thousand items in the last decade, as global discourse on art restitution and repatriation has gathered force. “It’s a thing of joy that the objects are coming in our time,” Mark Olaitan, the curator of Nigeria’s National Museum, Benin City, told me in November. At first, many Nigerians could hardly believe that they would be the generation to see the items’ return: “People saw it as fables.”

The question of how to receive the returning bronzes fell to the Benin Dialogue Group, a coalition formed in 2007 and made up of delegates from major international museums and officials from the Nigerian government and Benin’s Royal Court. In 2020 the group’s local partner, the newly established nonprofit Legacy Restoration Trust, announced plans for a state-of-the-art museum where the objects could be conserved and made available to the public. The institution, which is now known as the Museum of West African Art (MOWAA), quickly won promises of financial support from European organizations and from the government of Edo State, of which Benin City is the capital. Phillip Ihenacho, MOWAA’s director, initially envisioned it as a place both for repatriated objects, starting with the bronzes, and for work by contemporary artists. “When we started, it was sort of a dual mission,” he told me last year. “Then we rapidly discovered how emotional and intense and far from clear a lot of the restitution discussion is.”

By the time MOWAA was set to open its doors to the public last November, a protracted struggle had rerouted the returning bronzes: they had instead ended up in the oba’s palace and Benin’s National Museum, a long-standing institution under the auspices of Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments (NCMM). Yet that didn’t stop protesters from disrupting MOWAA’s preview opening for select guests—European and American patrons and diplomats, Nigerian literati and elite, and members of the international press, myself included—by storming the grounds and heckling attendees, accusing the institution of a lack of transparency and of bypassing traditional authorities in its quest to claim the bronzes. Almost a year later, the museum remains closed indefinitely, with viewings only by appointment. The bronzes have finally come home—but home has proved to be a fraught idea.

The tension over who should receive the bronzes first became evident in the strained relationship between Godwin Obaseki, the former governor of Edo State, and the current oba, Ewuare II. The oba asserts—and many Bini people agree—that the bronzes rightfully belong to him because most of them were commissioned by obas and crafted by the guilds in the royal court. In 2018 Obaseki’s government, at the oba’s urging, announced plans to house the bronzes in a “Benin Royal Museum” that would exist independently of the NCMM and have more advanced infrastructure for displaying the items than the Benin National Museum has; construction was to be funded by Benin Dialogue Group members like the British Museum and Germany’s Museum am Rothenbaum. But the institution never materialized, reportedly due to disputes between Obaseki and Ewuare II over funding, location, and control. While the oba continues to push for the creation of the royal museum, Obaseki soon pivoted to advocating for MOWAA’s establishment instead.

The monarchy and its supporters did not look kindly on Obaseki’s promotion of a project that competed with the oba’s own bid for donors. At a press conference in July 2021 Ewuare II denounced the governor for backing MOWAA: “The right and only legitimate destination for the artifacts to be repatriated, as already pronounced by my father, is under the aegis of the Benin Royal Museum that will be sited within the precincts of the Palace of the Oba of Benin, from where they were looted.”

The conflict between the two men arguably has its origins as far back as 1897: Obaseki is the direct descendant of Agho Obaseki, who was appointed acting prime minister of the Benin kingdom by the British after they exiled the sitting oba, Ovonramwen. In 1914, when the British merged the Southern Nigerian Protectorate (which included the Benin kingdom) and the Northern Nigerian Protectorate to form the Nigeria colony, they elevated Agho to the position of iyase—the highest-ranking chief title in the Benin kingdom. Agho’s ascension put him at odds with Oba Eweka II, who had succeeded Ovonramwen after he died in exile. Obaseki’s forefather is remembered as a shrewd, clearsighted figure who kept the kingdom from being entirely subsumed by the colony, negotiating to maintain features of the monarchy’s administration. But he is also derided, even today, as a self-serving traitor to the oba dynasty.

The oba’s part in contemporary events may surprise outsiders. Despite lacking any constitutional power, he holds influence over many facets of life in Benin’s heartland: he remains the divine leader according to the traditional religion; customarily presides over, or is at least consulted on, local affairs, including land disputes; and acts as the primary custodian of Benin’s culture and heritage. And in the case of MOWAA, he made it clear that he was discontented with a cultural institution ostensibly being built in service of that heritage. (The Benin Royal Council, which reports to the oba, did not return requests for comment; the oba himself rarely gives interviews for cultural and religious reasons.)

In addition to the oba’s disapproval, the museum had to confront the reality that Benin City is hardly the natural place for such an institution. It lacks the infrastructure of Abuja, Nigeria’s capital, or Lagos, a cultural metropolis in its own right—both of which boast a wealth of modern galleries and other arts establishments, as well as scores of affluent potential benefactors with international connections. In Benin, by contrast, despite an ongoing, rapid process of urban renewal, MOWAA is an anomaly.

The fight over the museum was encapsulated by a disagreement over its name: at first MOWAA was to be called the Edo Museum of West African Art, for the Nigerian state where it is located. “Edo” is the autochthonous name for the region’s people; they were christened the “Bini” by the Portuguese, who arrived in the kingdom in the fifteenth century and derived the name from that of the kingdom’s capital, Ubini. But it seemed that to the oba and many others, the inclusion of Edo in the proposed name both signified a blessing that hadn’t been given and represented a shift in focus toward the broader region and away from Benin City. Ihenacho confirmed that the state’s name was dropped due to “strained relationships” between Obaseki’s and Ewuare’s camps.

In March 2023 Nigeria’s outgoing president, the late Muhammadu Buhari, took the monarchy’s side in the contretemps, decreeing that the bronzes would be returned to the oba’s custody. His announcement dismayed both the NCMM, then active in the return negotiations, and some of the Western stakeholders who had backed MOWAA’s construction. One unnamed NCMM official told the BBC that Buhari’s statement was “written by someone who doesn’t understand how museums work.” The decision effectively undercut the NCMM’s ability to negotiate for the bronzes on Nigeria’s behalf. It may also hinder the agency in future international negotiations by setting a precedent that could encourage other customary rulers to assert claims over precolonial art and objects. 

One half of MOWAA’s dual mission had officially become moot. But construction continued even without the bronzes or the oba’s blessing. Foreign backers like GIZ, a German enterprise that funds sustainable development, and the Mellon Foundation were still willing to support the museum as a home for contemporary West African artists and arts education. Yet no one involved with the project seems to have entirely anticipated the confusion and suspicion that the oba’s opposition would stoke in the region. Some people didn’t understand that the museum would not, after all, host the bronzes, and resented it for claiming an inheritance that they felt belonged with the oba; others, aware of the change, questioned why the project was still going ahead and speculated about a concealed financial motive. “There’s a lot of people thinking that this is a private business where money is going to be made, that the former governor has some financial interest,” Ihenacho told me. “Some of this stuff you hear anecdotally, you don’t really believe that people think it—until you see that people do.”

I landed in Benin City for MOWAA’s opening last November to frantic messages from colleagues and public relations personnel telling me to come at once—or not at all. Instinctively, I did the former. When I arrived some of the protesters—mostly young men who couldn’t have been older than twenty-five—had reassembled after being dispersed by the city’s police a few hours earlier. Some still had sticks or stones in their hands and were wearing red hats, a nod to the coral cap worn by the oba and high-ranking chiefs in the kingdom. A handful of bored-looking police officers stood nearby. On my way to the entrance, I spoke to a group of protesters in Delta Pidgin; my own family is Urhobo and from Delta State, which borders Edo, and the languages share enough vocabulary that we were able to communicate. They let me pass without the heckling they had directed at other guests.

The protests continued after I entered the museum, and later forced many of us who were there that day to exit in small groups through a side entrance. They spurred MOWAA to cancel the rest of the events planned for the preview, including a historical site tour, campus talks, and a day-long symposium on African art. The vast majority of the protesters were poor or working class; many were disaffected youth, and some were members of local social and cultural groups loosely affiliated with the Palace. None would speak to me on the record, but they made their dissatisfaction known on Nigerian television news and social media, decrying what they considered the museum’s lack of clarity about its purpose and its failure to respect the oba’s authority. They insinuated that MOWAA was profiting from their history and their land without their consent. Edobor Osazee, Coordinator of the Coalition of Benin Socio-Cultural Organisations (CBSCO), told Nigeria’s Television Continental News that the process by which the museum was established was “cunning and crafty.” In the same segment another unidentified protester said of MOWAA, “They know what they are doing. They want to catch us unaware and that is why they came on Sunday because most of us went to church. But thank God and our ancestors who was able to awaken us and say we should go and stop them.”

Nevertheless, the preview’s attendees appeared absorbed. I was captivated by the modern, rammed-earth exterior of the building, which was designed by the renowned Ghanaian-British architect David Adjaye. (He received the commission before he was accused of sexual misconduct by three of his former employees in 2023.) Inside, the 48,000-square-foot museum was full of gleaming galleries and boasted a 180-seat auditorium and a state-of-the art lab devoted to material science, archaeological research, and art restoration. Archaeologists affiliated with the museum had already begun extensive excavations of Edo artifacts in the city and started conducting scientific analyses on objects from across West Africa.

The exhibition on display in the atrium was a limited survey of West African history as told through objects and sculptures representing different nations and ethnic groups. The majority were of Yoruba origin, reflecting the group’s cultural dominance and ethnic privilege—and, arguably, the Yoruba’s longstanding tradition of cultural exchange. I paused in front of the copper mask of Obalufon, the third ooni, or traditional ruler, of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the ancient city and spiritual home of the Yoruba people, located in what is now Osun State. The early fourteenth-century mask, which has hollow, almond-shaped eyes and small, round punctures around the mouth and chin—“possibly designed for attaching a ceremonial beard,” as the description noted—was on loan from the National Museum’s Lagos division. There wasn’t much to be found of the Binis here. I wondered if this would make the protesters outside, and MOWAA’s local detractors in general, more or less displeased.

When I spoke with MOWAA’s modern and contemporary curator, Aindrea Emelife, the following day, she defended the museum’s collection. “Whilst there wasn’t such presence of Benin objects, there was presence of Benin history,” she said. She pointed to the inclusion of a piece by the artist Isaac Emokpae that engages with the work of his late father, the famed Erhabor. She also noted that while about 70 percent of the works on display are Nigerian, the museum has also tried to represent other countries in West Africa “because quite frankly—and I can say this because I’m Nigerian—we do take up the conversation.”

The preview’s main attraction was “Nigeria Imaginary: Homecoming,” an exhibition of work by eleven artists, seven of whom were shown in Nigeria’s pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale. That show was criticized for featuring only one artist who lives and works primarily in Nigeria—a problem Emelife sought to rectify by adding four more. MOWAA described the art on view as focusing on “questions of nationhood,” though they defined the word broadly. Toyin Ojih Odutola’s Lęhin Mgbede (Before +After the Evening’s Performance) (2023–2024), for example, a diptych using layered pastel, charcoal, and graphite on linen, depicts a cast of characters preceding and following some unseen event. It is a testament to Odutola’s personal experience of mourning her grandmother that at the same time conveys a transethnic Nigerian sensibility: our ancestors, it emphasizes, remain constant guides even as we transition between life and death. Yinka Shonibare’s Monument to the Restitution of the Mind and Soul (2024), meanwhile, consists of 153 clay replicas of the stolen Benin treasures along with a Batik-patterned bust of Sir Harry Rawson, the British naval officer who led the 1897 attack.

One of the Nigeria-based artists added to the show was Isaac Emokpae (he splits his time between Lagos and Reading, England). Walking through the galleries, I spotted him looking delighted, taking a picture of his mixed-media painting Sarkin Amina (The Story of a Monarch) (2025). It’s a reinterpretation of the story of Queen Amina, the sixteenth-century leader of the precolonial Hausa Kingdom of Zazzau, now in the northern Nigerian state of Zaria. As the first woman to rule Zazzau—remaining unmarried while doing so—she commanded formidable military campaigns that expanded her kingdom’s size and riches. Emokpae explained that he was drawn to Queen Amina because, like Queen Idia, she defied the constraints placed on women and left a legacy in the place she ruled. From the city walls she constructed to the trade routes she forged, “Amina is very influential in how northern Nigeria became the way we know it today.”

Sarkin Amina also references a 1976 oil painting of the same subject, Queen Amina of Zaria, by Emokpae’s father. The older Emokpae shows Queen Amina twice: on one side of the canvas, she rides on horseback with sword in hand, leading her soldiers into battle; her portrait gazes out from the other side, in a muted red dress and orange head covering, with a phlegmatic disposition. In the younger Emokpae’s interpretation she wears the colors of royalty, a long blue dress and velvet head covering of deep violet. At her feet appear to be her subjects, while just behind her are guards in red tagelmust and litham—the cloth mouth-veils and turbans traditionally worn by men in parts of the Sahara region. In a scene visible over her shoulder, a girl—Amina as a child—play-fights with a boy, using sticks as swords. When he spoke to me in January from his studio in Reading, Emokpae told me that a detail in that background, a praying mantis on a clay sill behind the queen’s guards, represents her sexual independence. (The insect “eats a male counterpart after mating,” he pointed out.)

Later it occurred to me that Queen Amina could also be understood as a symbol of Nigerian national unity, a way to declare that the history of northern Nigeria belongs, in a sense, to all of us. In “Nigeria Imaginary: Homecoming,” first conceived for an international audience, I saw MOWAA’s aspiration to serve as a home for contemporary global art—but also its ambition to take part in remaking Nigerian nationhood amid imperial histories that assembled diverse groups into a single polity. This very objective honors the history of the Bini, whose kingdom, empire that it was, always comprised a multitude of different peoples.

But even if MOWAA is very much for Nigeria and Nigerians, is it really for the Bini? It was notable that the preview was timed to follow on the heels of Lagos’s tenth international art fair, ART x Lagos. Many guests, myself included, attended the larger event before traveling to the MOWAA opening, only an hour’s flight away. Press previews, of course, are never intended for the public; still, save for the volunteers, this one was almost entirely a gathering of outsiders—a detail easily misconstrued by residents. Some locals clearly took from our presence that MOWAA may be in their home, but it is not their museum.

Ihenacho told me that he regrets not communicating the museum’s mission more clearly. “Maybe we should try to speak more loudly about what we are but also what we are not,” he told me. “Much misperception still exists about who we are, about how we originated, about who has an interest.” Perhaps MOWAA could have taken greater care to reach locals in forums they frequent—including on WhatsApp, where all Nigerian news and gossip lives many lifetimes. They could also have brought more local artists into the museum’s orbit. When I spoke to young artists in Benin City, many seemed to feel that, as the budding contemporary painter Derek Jahyém Jombo-Ogboi put it, residents “didn’t have a say.”

Certainly, the MOWAA preview made a sharp contrast with a truly local arts event that began on the same day: the Black Muse Arts Festival, put on by the internationally acclaimed, Edo State–born artist and writer Victor Ehikhamenor. The festival took place in a park in Benin City’s residential Iyekogba neighborhood. Entry was free; attendees drifted through the open, convivial gathering and ate “small chops,” jollof, and sweets from local businesses. A young multidisciplinary artist from Benin City, Osaru Obaseki (no direct relation to the governor), won first prize for Coat of Many Lines, a pair of casted bronze busts. People remarked on how the event had beautified the neighborhood, bringing not only the sculptural installations—which remained until April of this year—but also a forty-nine-foot vaulted pavilion made from bamboo, the work of the Nigerian architect James Inedu-George.

MOWAA’s future, meanwhile, remains uncertain. According to Nigerian news networks, Ewuare II visited the governor of Edo state, Monday Okpebholo, two days before the disastrous preview and implored him to order a full investigation into MOWAA’s finances. Okpebholo reemphasized his commitment to creating a Benin Royal Museum. “The issue of MOWAA is over,” he told the oba and the rest of the audience. “It was a gift to Your Majesty, and it will be restored as such”—which is to say, converted into the royal museum that Obaseki’s government had first imagined back in 2018. (The royal palace hasn’t released any formal statement on MOWAA in the months since.)

The day after the preview, Okpebholo reportedly revoked the museum’s Certificate of Occupancy, nullifying its right to use the land on which it sits. The Nigerian press suggested that the governor wanted to restore the land to its previous purpose as the site of the Benin Central Hospital, although that explanation seems unconvincing: the hospital’s services were relocated after its facilities were deemed inadequate in 2021. So far the museum remains in place, neither open to the public nor shut down by the state. It is an institution in abeyance. 

Still, the debacle does not seem beyond solving. In late November, President Bola Tinubu set up a committee to bring together representatives of the oba, leading officials from the cultural sector (including Hannatu Musawa, Nigeria’s Minister of Art, Culture, Tourism, and the Creative Economy), and French and German emissaries. The group has been tasked with submitting a “comprehensive framework for the permanent resolution” of the dispute directly to the president, though is has not been given a deadline, and the art ministry did not respond to multiple requests for comment. One might hope that Nigerians, who were once a people loath to broadcast embarrassments on this scale, would be determined—even after years of incompetent governance—to save face by any possible means.

To succeed, MOWAA will need the oba’s support, or at least his acquiescence, which would encourage the city’s inhabitants to view the institution in a new light. In November, on the day it announced its indefinite closure—the day before it was supposed to open to the public—MOWAA posted a detailed statement to its website aiming to “clarify recent misconceptions circulating about its mission, holdings, and role,” emphasizing that they held the oba in “the highest esteem,” and stressing that the museum “does not hold, nor have we ever claimed title” to the bronzes. In February Ihenacho personally released another statement proposing listening sessions to be held across Nigeria and West Africa from March to May, to help the museum “consider how cultural institutions can be grounded, responsive, and accountable to their publics.” 

Benin history is full of disputes between obas and chiefs, often with much more at stake than a contemporary art museum. The oba dynasty has survived precisely because it knows how to adapt to its surroundings while maintaining its authority. MOWAA, if its most influential stakeholders have a sense of humor, might even create an exhibit to honor this feature of Bini history; it could nod to ancient Benin’s guilds by commissioning works from artists in the city. Such an exhibition could perhaps include contemporary brass masks and figurines that would tell the story of the obas. That way, MOWAA could end up displaying some Benin Bronzes after all.

The historic bronzes, meanwhile, have been arriving in waves since 2022, to the unbridled joy of Benin City residents. The local press documented the oba dancing when wooden and bronze stools arrived from Germany in 2024; according to Olaitan, people throughout the city were equally jubilant. Over one hundred artifacts, mainly from the Netherlands, were already on display at Benin’s National Museum as of last November. Hundreds more will return this year from England and elsewhere, all legally owned by the oba.

When I visited the National Museum during my trip to Benin City, the brilliance of the returned bronzes was slightly dimmed by their surroundings. The placards describing the items were terse and printed on flimsy-looking white cardboard. I wondered how much care had been taken in the placement of each item; the masks tell a story, but their display did not. The facilities paled beside those I’d just seen at MOWAA. I felt that the Benin Royal Museum could not come to fruition soon enough.

And yet among the many marvelous objects—meticulously articulated plaques of obas and warrior chiefs in ceremonial regalia, ritual and fighting swords, life-like cockerels and crocodiles, and more—was an ivory mask of Queen Idia, repatriated in 2022. The British Museum still holds one likeness; this one was repatriated by the Linden Museum in Stuttgart, Germany, though the placard incorrectly stated that it had been returned by the Smithsonian. The top of this Idia’s forehead is wrapped in coral beads, separating the decorative pattern of her headdress from the incision lines just above her eyes, marks she is said to have obtained around the time of her marriage to Oba Ozolua, Oba Ésigie’s father, and which supposedly furnished her with arcane powers. She wears the stern and watchful expression of a matriarch. I was happy to see her there, in her home.
